title: Adab with parents
hook: a man asks who most deserves his good company, and hears one answer three times

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of the market, and your line: easy in dealing. Today, the adab closest to home.

Your mother. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Then your father. Abu Hurayrah reports the exchange in Sahih al-Bukhari. A man had asked the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, which of all people most deserves his good companionship. He asked four times, and the answer didn't move until the fourth. Not a speech, not a list of virtues. One word, said again and again, until it couldn't be missed. Today's adab sits inside that repetition.
screen: `WHO MOST DESERVES MY COMPANY?` → `YOUR MOTHER. YOUR MOTHER. YOUR MOTHER.` → `THEN YOUR FATHER.`

segments.voice: Why say it three times? The hadith itself doesn't explain, but the Qur'an gives a picture. In surah Luqman, in Pickthall's translation: "His mother beareth him in weakness upon weakness." The verse goes on to the weaning. The repetition sounds like a debt counted out loud. And the father isn't dropped. He's named, and his place is real. Then how. In al-Isra, kindness to parents comes right after the command to worship none but Allah. When parents grow old, the verse says, don't even say uff to them, the smallest sound of irritation. Pickthall renders the rest: "speak unto them a gracious word." And the image of the wing: "lower unto them the wing of submission through mercy." A bird lowering its wing over its young; here the grown child does it for the parent. The verse gives a du'a too: "My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little." The adab has an honest edge. Surah Luqman says that if parents push a child to associate partners with Allah, the child shouldn't obey, but should still keep company with them kindly in this world. Disagreement doesn't cancel kindness. So adab with parents isn't only obedience. It's company, a gracious word, a lowered wing, and a du'a, with the mother named three times.
screen: `WEAKNESS UPON WEAKNESS.` · `NOT EVEN A SIGH OF IRRITATION.` · `THE WING LOWERED THROUGH MERCY.` · `DISAGREE, AND STAY KIND.`

segments.voice: Bring your mother to mind, or whoever mothered you, and if she's living and you can reach her, picture a call today and one gracious word you'd say. If she has died, a hadith in Sahih Muslim counts a child who prays for a parent among the good that continues after death; if you pray, you can say the line from al-Isra: my Lord, have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little. If the relationship is hard, simply hold her in mind with whatever mercy is possible today.
Adab with parents. Good companionship, gentle speech and a lowered wing of mercy, with the mother named three times before the father. Today's word.
Your line: mother, three times. And your father too. Tomorrow, the adab with neighbors.

howItsDone: Muslims treat kindness to parents as a duty that follows worship of Allah, cite the hadith naming the mother three times, and recite "My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little" for their parents, living or dead.

chat.says: My parents and I disagree about faith. Do I still owe them kindness?
options: Yes. Surah Luqman says don't obey in associating partners, but keep kind company with them.
No. Once you disagree about faith, the duty of kindness to parents ends.
Only if you agree to everything they ask, including what goes against Allah.
